clue.text: Hideous thing in story, most crude

indicators.note: something crude is rough and unrefined, so the letters are taken in an unpolished, jumbled order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A reviewer complains of a hideous character in a tale told in the crudest possible way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in story, most' reads as part of the surface sentence, but all three words are the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A monstrosity is something grotesquely ugly, an outrageously unsightly object or building.

clue.text: Both cricket sides constantly interrupted

blocks.note: in cricket the two halves of the field are the on side and the off side

explanation.surface: A cricket match keeps being stopped, for both teams, by the weather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sides' looks like the two teams, but in cricket the field itself is split into the on (leg) side and the off side.
explanation.definitionFit: Something on-off keeps stopping and starting, so it is repeatedly broken off, like an intermittent relationship.

clue.text: Released, fixed price about right

indicators.note: about means going round, so the second word wraps itself around the next letter

blocks.note: fixed in place means set
a fee is a price charged
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A goods item is released for sale at a fixed price that seems about right.
explanation.definitionFit: To set someone free is to liberate them, the past form matching released as a participle.

clue.text: Keep mother in check

indicators.note: in places one word inside another, as a parent sits within a restraint

blocks.note: to check is to rein, as a rider restrains a horse
ma is a familiar word for mother

explanation.surface: Advice to restrain an overbearing mother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep' and 'check' both look like verbs about control; only 'Keep' is the definition, in the sense of stay.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep, as in keep quiet or keep calm, is to stay or continue in a state, which is to remain.

clue.text: Fish, ridiculous in a dress!

indicators.note: ridiculous suggests something absurd and out of order, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims that a fish looks ridiculous dressed up in a frock.
explanation.definitionFit: Sardines are small oily fish of the herring family, usually sold tinned.

clue.text: Consideration, however, close to redundant

indicators.note: close to means the end of the word, so only its final letter is used

blocks.note: though can mean however, as in 'he did, though'
the final letter of redundant

explanation.surface: A manager gives some consideration to a worker, though they are close to being laid off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'close to' reads as 'nearly' in the surface, but it means the last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Thought is careful reflection or attention given to something, the same as consideration.

clue.text: Ridiculous concern for devilry

blocks.note: funny can mean absurd or laughable
a concern is a firm or business

explanation.surface: A ridiculous company set up to do mischief.
explanation.definitionFit: Funny business is mischief or shady trickery, which is roughly what devilry means.

clue.text: Dorothy's companion in dress let hair down?

indicators.note: in puts the companion inside the garment, as one would be dressed in it

blocks.note: a gown is a dress
Toto is Dorothy's dog in The Wizard of Oz

explanation.surface: Dorothy's friend dresses up and lets loose at a party.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'let hair down' is a loose, idiomatic definition rather than an exact equivalent.
explanation.definitionFit: To go to town is to do something lavishly and without restraint, much as letting your hair down means relaxing inhibitions.

clue.text: Bad job: bone to chew on, perhaps?

blocks.note: first meaning: a mess, something done very badly
second meaning, read literally: what a pet hound might be given first thing in the morning

explanation.walkthrough: The second half is a playful literal reading of the idiom, hence 'perhaps' and the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog's breakfast is British slang for a botched mess, and literally a canine's morning meal might include a bone.

clue.text: Umpteen barnacles on another tanker, first of all — vessel going under

indicators.note: first of all asks for the first letter of every one of the preceding words

blocks.note: initial letters of the five words

explanation.surface: Countless barnacles cling to a tanker before it sinks.
explanation.walkthrough: A U-boat is a German submarine of the World Wars.
explanation.definitionFit: A U-boat is a submarine, a vessel designed to travel beneath the surface of the sea.

clue.text: Old chronicler has stuff to write about, old sport

indicators.note: writing something about-face means setting it down back to front

blocks.note: to stuff is to cram
O is a standard abbreviation for old
polo is a sport played on horseback

explanation.surface: An old writer has plenty of material about an ancient sporting chap.
explanation.walkthrough: MARCO POLO, the Venetian traveller, wrote an account of his journeys to Asia. 'old sport' looks like a form of address, but splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Marco Polo's account of his travels to the court of Kublai Khan makes him a medieval chronicler.

clue.text: Egyptian queen jogging in, fitter having run around Egypt's capital

indicators.note: jogging shakes things about, so these letters are jostled into a new order
a capital is the head letter of a word, so only its first one is taken
to run around something is to encircle it, so the jumbled letters surround what follows

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
the opening letter of Egypt

explanation.surface: An ancient queen of Egypt gets fitter by jogging around the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital' here means a capital letter, not a city.
explanation.definitionFit: Nefertiti was the wife of the pharaoh Akhenaten and a celebrated queen of ancient Egypt.

clue.text: Vile group of 144

blocks.note: first meaning: disgusting, revolting
second meaning: twelve dozen

explanation.walkthrough: The two parts are unrelated meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is an adjective for something disgusting and a noun for a quantity of twelve dozen.

clue.text: Batter a selection of cold foods

blocks.note: first meaning, a verb: to strike repeatedly
second meaning: a spread from which diners help themselves

explanation.walkthrough: 'Batter' looks like a cooking ingredient, matching the food theme, but it is the verb meaning to pound.
explanation.definitionFit: To buffet is to knock about, as waves do, and a buffet is a self-service meal laid out on a table.

clue.text: Four neighbouring characters, one entering wood — dark entertainment

indicators.note: entering means going inside, so these letters are placed within the tree

blocks.note: fir is a timber tree
four letters that sit side by side in the alphabet
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Four neighbours, one of them going into a wood, sounds like the start of a dark thriller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'characters' means letters; any four in a row would do, so the crossing letters choose them.
explanation.definitionFit: Film noir is a genre of bleak, shadowy crime movies, so it is literally entertainment that is dark.

clue.text: Hybrid of rodent and ox, very close!

indicators.note: a hybrid blends things together, so the letters are mixed into one new form

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone marvels at a cross between a rat and an ox, a near thing.
explanation.definitionFit: Next door means in the adjacent house, so it is used as an adjective or adverb for something immediately beside you.

clue.text: Turn off course over Channel for bomber, for example?

blocks.note: to warp is to bend out of true or deviate
a lane is a channel or route, as for shipping

explanation.surface: A wartime bomber veers off course while crossing the English Channel.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' means the first piece sits above the second. 'Channel' looks like the English Channel but is just a route.
explanation.definitionFit: A bomber is one type of military aircraft, so it is an example of the general class, as the question mark flags.

clue.text: Nuts, alas, mistaken for fruit

indicators.note: mistaken means wrong, so these letters are arranged in a different order than given

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone sorts dried snacks and sighs that nuts were taken for dried fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuts' and 'fruit' both look like foods, but 'Nuts' is only letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Sultanas are dried seedless grapes, a common dried fruit used in baking.

clue.text: Maybe a bit less topping?

indicators.note: less topping means without its top, so the word loses its first letter

blocks.note: a particle is a tiny bit

explanation.surface: A diner asks for slightly less topping on their pizza.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is by example: 'a' is the indefinite article in grammar, hence 'Maybe'.
explanation.definitionFit: In grammar the words a, an and the are determiners called articles, so 'a' is one instance.

clue.text: African country ready once?

blocks.note: first meaning: a nation in West Africa
second meaning: an old British coin, ready being slang for cash

explanation.walkthrough: Ready, or the readies, is British slang for cash; a guinea was a gold coin worth 21 shillings, no longer minted, hence 'once'.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs to a West African state and to a former British coin, a form of money from the past.

clue.text: Parvenu happy before initiation

blocks.note: feeling up means cheerful
an initiation is a beginning or start

explanation.surface: A newcomer to society is delighted before his induction.
explanation.definitionFit: An upstart is a social climber who has suddenly risen in status, which is what a parvenu is.

clue.text: Pianist originally covering for violinist, perhaps

indicators.note: originally points to the origin, the very first letter of the word

blocks.note: first letter of pianist
a layer is a covering

explanation.surface: A pianist steps in to cover for an absent violinist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'covering for' reads as deputising, but 'covering' is a noun piece and 'for' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: A violinist is one kind of musician who plays an instrument, an example of the broader term.

clue.text: Group of nine fishermen made redundant then?

blocks.note: first meaning: an ensemble of nine performers
second meaning, read cryptically: workers left with nothing to fish with

explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as NO NET: fishermen without a net would be out of work.
explanation.definitionFit: A nonet is a musical composition or ensemble for nine players, like a nine-piece band.

clue.text: Tongue out, eat!

blocks.note: Polish is a language, and tongue means language
off can mean out, as of a light or a game

explanation.surface: A parent tells a child to stop sticking their tongue out and eat their dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tongue out' looks like rude behaviour at the table, but 'Tongue' means a language.
explanation.definitionFit: To polish off food is to finish it all quickly, an idiom for eating the lot.

clue.text: Unfashionable affair, better

blocks.note: something out is no longer in fashion
a do is a party or social affair

explanation.surface: An unfashionable affair that was nonetheless better than expected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'better' looks like an adjective but is a verb, meaning to surpass.
explanation.definitionFit: To better someone is to surpass or exceed them, the same as to outdo them.

clue.text: Doing porridge, frantically mixed up?

blocks.note: surface reading: someone stirring a pan of oatmeal in a frenzy
setter's reading: serving a prison sentence and driven mad by confinement

explanation.walkthrough: 'Doing porridge' is British slang for serving time in prison, and stir is slang for jail; mixing porridge also means stirring it.
explanation.definitionFit: Stir-crazy describes someone made restless or deranged by long confinement, originally in prison.

clue.text: Might they take part in musical, to sing?

definitions.text: Might they take part in musical, to sing?

indicators.note: take part in hints that only a portion of the next words is used, a run of consecutive letters

blocks.note: a run of letters spanning the three words

explanation.surface: Wondering whether certain singers will join the cast of a musical.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition, as singers of this voice part would take part in a musical, and the wordplay is also contained in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Altos are singers with a low female or high male voice, who would indeed sing parts in a musical.

clue.text: Second-rate, I gathered, lack of respect on church property

definitions.text: lack of respect on church property

indicators.note: gathered suggests collecting things in a heap, so the letters are assembled anew

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone notices shoddy, disrespectful behaviour in a churchyard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I gathered' reads as 'I understood', but 'I' is part of the letters and 'gathered' signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Desecration is the violation of something sacred, such as vandalising a church or graveyard.
